speaker: Pieter van der Does
title: Adyen success story: Pieter van der Does building one of Europe’s largest fintech unicorns
question: In late-stage private companies, why do repeated secondary share sales eventually stop working as a way to stay independent instead of going public?
guest: We got high offers and didn't accept them, or at least they seemed high at the time. What we did do is allow new investors in so that there was some liquidity, through secondaries. That helped so that the investors felt the financial success, that they could actually spend that money, and that it was visible to them rather than just theoretical. But what we also found out is that the first secondary gave us, say, two years before there was a need for doing something. Then the next one gave us a year, and then the third one gave us half a year. You saw that the medicine became less powerful with the valuation of the company going up. So that was a contributing factor to saying maybe it's good if at a certain point everybody can just decide for themselves what they want to do with their shares.

points.core: Early secondaries buy patience by turning paper wealth into spendable cash.
points.note: Accept: tender offers or secondary sales let early investors realize tangible returns so they do not force an acquisition. Do not credit: generic statements that investors want liquidity.

points.core: Each successive secondary round buys a shorter interval before liquidity pressure returns.
points.note: Accept: diminishing half-life of secondary rounds (e.g., two years, then one year, then six months) as intervals between liquidity demands compress. Do not credit: claiming secondaries fail immediately or only work once.

points.core: Rising company valuations weaken the relief each private secondary transaction provides.
points.note: Accept: higher valuations expand locked-up paper gains so periodic private sales become less effective at appeasing shareholders. Do not credit: generic complaints about administrative or legal costs of secondaries.

points.core: Going public eventually becomes necessary so shareholders can manage exits independently.
points.note: Accept: an IPO acts as a technical liquidity mechanism allowing each investor to sell or hold on their own schedule rather than relying on company-orchestrated rounds. Do not credit: generic IPO benefits like brand awareness or raising primary capital.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Secondary sales and tender offers relieve the pressure to go public, but they only move existing shares between holders; they don't solve the underlying problems, which grow with each round.

First, the scale outgrows the buyer pool. As the company's valuation rises, the amount of liquidity that employees and early investors need grows into the tens of billions, and only public markets have that depth. Private buyers also demand a discount for illiquidity and eventually need an exit themselves.

Second, early venture funds have fixed lifespans and must return cash to their own investors, so partial liquidity at a discount stops satisfying them.

Third, each sale spreads the shareholder base. Once a company has enough holders of record (2,000 in the US), it must file public-style reports anyway, removing much of the benefit of staying private.

Fourth, pricing becomes strained. Without a continuous market, valuations go stale, tender prices raise the tax valuation of employee stock options, and the stock is a weak currency for acquisitions and hiring.

Finally, secondaries typically raise no money for the company itself, so large capital needs still push it toward an IPO.

points.why: The response credits secondary sales with easing IPO pressure by giving early investors cash they can distribute.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Repeated secondary share sales eventually falter because cumulative liquidity demand outgrows what private buyers can absorb. As valuations climb and early venture funds hit fund-life deadlines to return capital, the supply of shares from investors and long-tenured employees overwhelms the narrow pool of crossover and secondary buyers. Those buyers themselves underwrite to an eventual public exit, so staying private indefinitely leads to rationed tender caps, steeper valuation discounts, or costly governance concessions, while broader secondary trading risks breaching SEC shareholder limits that trigger mandatory public reporting anyway.

Compensation and corporate finance add further pressure. Late-stage companies rely heavily on restricted stock units; allowing them to vest in tender offers creates massive cash tax-withholding bills for the company, whereas keeping them unvested hurts retention and risks grant expirations. Negotiated secondary prices also push up 409A valuations, reducing upside for new hires without providing continuous price discovery. Finally, episodic tenders raise no primary capital and leave private stock too illiquid to serve as credible acquisition currency.

points.why: The response describes pressure to sell but never explains how early secondaries turn paper gains into spendable cash and buy shareholder patience.
The response describes growing liquidity demand without saying that each successive round buys less time before pressure returns.
The response identifies rising valuations as a factor that makes private buyers less able to meet shareholder demand for liquidity.
quotes: As valuations climb and early venture funds hit fund-life deadlines to return capital, the supply of shares from investors and long-tenured employees overwhelms the narrow pool of crossover and secondary buyers.

points.why: The response mentions an eventual public exit without explaining how public trading lets shareholders sell or hold on their own schedules.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Secondary sales, usually company-run tender offers, move existing shares from employees and early investors to new buyers. They provide liquidity, but they don't fix the underlying pressures, and several limits build over time.

First, the pool of buyers shrinks. As the valuation climbs into the tens or hundreds of billions, each tender needs fewer, larger buyers willing to pay a high private price for illiquid, minority stock with little information or control. Buyers then demand discounts or special terms.

Second, the need for liquidity keeps growing. Early VC funds have roughly ten-year lives and must return cash to their own investors. Employee equity piles up, and RSUs may expire or create tax bills. Periodic, capped tenders can't fully meet those needs, which makes it harder to keep and recruit staff.

Third, secondaries raise little or no new money for the company. Firms with heavy capital needs, such as AI compute, eventually need public markets.

Finally, without public shares the company lacks a liquid currency for acquisitions. Growing shareholder counts and disclosure pressure also push it toward public-company obligations anyway.

So secondaries delay an IPO but rarely replace one.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Repeated secondary sales eventually break down as a substitute for an IPO because of regulatory limits, shrinking buyer appetite, and structural friction. In the U.S., selling shares to outside buyers steadily expands the cap table toward SEC thresholds—2,000 shareholders of record or 500 non-accredited investors—that trigger public-style financial reporting anyway, erasing much of the privacy advantage of staying independent. Even when companies use structured tender offers or special purpose vehicles to contain shareholder counts, the pool of institutional buyers willing to absorb massive blocks of illiquid stock with limited disclosure and no clear exit eventually thins out, forcing steeper discounts and tougher governance demands. Moreover, secondary transactions do not raise fresh capital for growth or provide liquid stock to use as currency for acquisitions. Over time, repeated tender offers also create administrative drag, complicate employee equity pricing and tax obligations, and leave late-stage investors pushing for the permanent liquidity and price discovery that only a public listing provides.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Repeated secondary sales let employees and early investors cash out, but each sale hands the need for an eventual exit to a new buyer. As more shareholders want to sell, the company has to keep finding buyers willing to tie up larger sums in shares that are hard to resell. If buyers lose confidence that they’ll have a reliable exit, they demand a steeper discount or stop buying. The company then has to accept a lower price, ration how much people can sell, or fund buybacks from its own cash.

A public listing can create a much broader market where shareholders can sell on their own schedule. There’s no fixed point at which secondaries fail. They become harder to sustain when the amount shareholders want to sell consistently exceeds what private buyers will absorb at a price sellers will accept.

points.why: Cashing out gives early holders tangible returns and shifts their need for an exit to incoming investors, buying the company time.
quotes: Repeated secondary sales let employees and early investors cash out, but each sale hands the need for an eventual exit to a new buyer.

points.why: The response describes growing difficulty finding buyers without saying that liquidity pressure returns sooner after each round.
The response links larger purchase commitments to more shareholders wanting to sell without explaining how rising valuations weaken the relief each sale provides.
The response identifies a public listing as a way for shareholders to choose when to sell independently of company-organized rounds.
quotes: A public listing can create a much broader market where shareholders can sell on their own schedule.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A secondary sale gives current shareholders cash, but the money goes to the sellers. The company gets no new capital, and the buyers eventually want a way to cash out too. Each round therefore depends on finding investors willing to take the shares at a price existing holders will accept. As more employees and early investors seek liquidity, buyers may demand a discount or wait for a clearer path to an exit.

An IPO creates an ongoing market where shareholders can sell over time and gives the company the option to raise capital by issuing new shares. A profitable company with patient owners can stay private indefinitely. Secondary sales stop working as a substitute for an IPO when demand to cash out regularly exceeds what private buyers or company-funded buybacks can absorb at an acceptable price.

The response identifies an ongoing public market as the mechanism that lets shareholders choose when to sell.
